items.text: **Bladder neck contracture (BNC)** is pathologic narrowing of the native bladder neck that causes bladder outlet obstruction. On WARWIKI, this page uses **BNC** primarily for the post-benign-outlet-procedure entity: scarring after TURP, bipolar TURP, HoLEP / endoscopic enucleation, laser vaporization, bladder-neck incision, or radiation-treated outlet tissue. Narrowing at the post-radical-prostatectomy vesicourethral anastomosis is handled separately as [vesicourethral anastomotic stenosis](/docs/clinical-conditions/03b-voiding-outlet/vesicourethral-anastomotic-stenosis) (VUAS).

The distinction is practical. In BNC, the prostate or prostatic fossa may still be present and the external sphincter is usually distal and intact. In VUAS, the prostate is absent and the scar sits immediately proximal to the membranous urethra, so every incision or reconstruction carries a higher continence penalty.

BNC incidence depends on the index outlet procedure, definition, and follow-up. Contemporary series after transurethral prostate surgery report BNC in roughly **1-6%** of patients (2% overall in one 1,008-patient series, 6.4% needing further surgery after TURP in another), with higher rates after bipolar TURP than enucleation in some cohorts.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)[[4]](#ref4)</sup> A meta-analysis of 28 RCTs found no significant difference in BNC between enucleation and TURP, so a lower enucleation rate should not be assumed.<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>

BNC is a circumferential scar response at the bladder neck. The reconstructive mechanism is familiar: ischemic mucosa, failed epithelial apposition, inflammation, urinary extravasation, infection, and repeated trauma heal by contraction rather than a stable epithelialized lumen.
Key contributors:
- **Small gland / small resection cavity** — less tissue removed, less funneling, and a tighter healing ring after TURP
- **Thermal injury** — coagulation at the bladder neck creates deeper ischemic fibrosis
- **Positive urine culture / UTI** — inflammation during healing increases scar burden
- **Repeat instrumentation** — catheter trauma, secondary transurethral intervention, and early reoperation add injury
- **Microvascular disease** — smoking, diabetes, hypertension, coronary disease, and radiation reduce tissue reserve
- **Under-treated outlet obstruction** — persistent high-pressure voiding can worsen symptoms even with a moderate scar

In TURP cohorts, smaller prostate volume, positive urine culture or preoperative UTI, and secondary transurethral intervention repeatedly emerge as practical warning signs.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)[[3]](#ref3)[[4]](#ref4)</sup>
- **Urinalysis and culture** — treat infection before incision
- **Uroflowmetry and PVR** — obstructive curve, low Qmax, elevated residual
- **Cystoscopy** — diagnostic test; defines lumen caliber, tissue quality, proximity to sphincter, stones, false passages, and catheterizability
- **RUG / VCUG** — useful when posterior urethral stricture, VUAS, or complex anatomy is possible
- **Urodynamics** — selected cases with underactive bladder, severe urgency, neurogenic concern, or discordant symptoms

If the patient has had radical prostatectomy, radical cystectomy with orthotopic neobladder, or a prostate-absent outlet, use the [VUAS framework](/docs/clinical-conditions/03b-voiding-outlet/vesicourethral-anastomotic-stenosis). A "bladder neck contracture" label after prostatectomy often hides a different continence and reconstruction problem.

In a 123-patient series (mostly BNC after radical prostatectomy, with or without radiation) using balloon dilation followed by deep bilateral Collins-knife incisions without intralesional agents, patency was **82.1% after one procedure** and **94.3% after two**, with two or more prior endoscopic procedures predicting failure.<sup>[[5]](#ref5)</sup>
- **Triamcinolone / steroid injection** — anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic; commonly injected into the incised scar quadrants
- **Mitomycin C** — off-label antifibrotic adjunct with heterogeneous retrospective results and potentially severe tissue injury

Mitomycin C has reported cumulative patency of about 75-90% after repeat procedures in recurrent BNC/VUAS series (65% and 58% after the first incision), with lower efficacy in radiated patients.<sup>[[7]](#ref7)[[11]](#ref11)</sup> These reports do not establish an advantage over incision alone. Serious events (7%) in the multicenter TURNS series included osteitis pubis, bladder-neck necrosis and rectourethral fistula, sometimes requiring cystectomy and diversion.<sup>[[11]](#ref11)</sup> The **EAU states that MMC should not be used outside a clinical trial** for non-traumatic posterior stenosis because of these serious events; it should not be presented as a routine adjunct.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)</sup>
- Ability to tolerate reconstruction vs chronic catheter / suprapubic tube

TUITMR adapts a Y-V-plasty concept endoscopically: scar is incised and healthy bladder mucosa is advanced transversely across the defect with endoscopic suturing. In 19 patients (47% BNC, 53% VUAS; median follow-up 6 months), patency was 89% after one procedure and 100% after two, without de novo incontinence; comparative and long-term data are lacking.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)</sup>

Robotic reconstruction is the usual next step after repeated endoscopic failure in a fit patient. A systematic review of ten small robotic case series (119 men, BNC and VUAS combined) reported pooled patency of 80% and pooled de novo incontinence of 17%, with wide ranges and short follow-up.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup> In a 21-patient robotic Y-V plasty series, the 15 men with BNC had no de novo stress incontinence and all de novo cases occurred after VUAS repair; stricture recurrence was 9.5% overall.<sup>[[16]](#ref16)</sup> Counsel that continence risk after repair is higher for VUAS, radiated tissue and prior sphincter compromise.
- In recurrent BNC or VUAS treated by incision with low-dose mitomycin C, overall success was 94% without radiation versus 76% with it.<sup>[[7]](#ref7)</sup>

- In the TURNS mitomycin series, serious adverse events (7%) included cases leading to cystectomy. Review summaries attribute the osteitis pubis cases to irradiated patients.<sup>[[11]](#ref11)[[12]](#ref12)</sup>
- Radionecrosis, cavitation, dystrophic calcification or fistula should shift the discussion toward diversion or subtotal prostatectomy rather than further endoscopy.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)</sup>
- TUITMR relies on healthy, mobile mucosa. Long stenoses with radionecrosis may lack the laxity needed for realignment.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)</sup>
Follow with symptoms, uroflow/PVR, and cystoscopy when symptoms recur. Failure patterns:
- **Early recurrence after one incision** — repeat incision may be reasonable.
- **Recurrence after two or more endoscopic procedures** — higher failure risk; begin reconstructive counseling.
- **Radiated recurrent BNC** — lower threshold for suprapubic diversion, urethral rest, imaging, and referral.
- **BNC plus incontinence** — stabilize outlet first; continence surgery before patency is durable is a trap.
